item.title: Northern Metropolis Development Ordinance gazetted
item.description:
​The Northern Metropolis Development Ordinance (the Ordinance) was gazetted today (November 20).
      
     The Northern Metropolis will be developed with the objectives of university town, innovation and technology, industry, and an environment suitable for living, work, and travel. It will be the main platform for Hong Kong to deeply engage in the development of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, and to actively integrate into and serve the overall national development, while serving as a strategic engine for Hong Kong to foster economic transformation and develop new quality productive forces. Upon passage by the Legislative Council (LegCo) at its third reading on November 12, the Ordinance carries great significance for Hong Kong in proactively aligning with the National 15th Five-Year Plan and implementing Hong Kong's First Five-Year Plan.
      
     The Ordinance provides the legal basis for various facilitation measures, covering town planning, land compensation, building works approvals, noise control as well as facilitating cross-boundary flows. It serves to expedite the development and construction processes, while helping enterprises to establish their presence in the Northern Metropolis. The Development Bureau and relevant bureaux are formulating the first batch of subsidiary legislation needed to implement such facilitation measures, with a view to tabling them for the LegCo's vetting in January and bringing them into effect in the first quarter of 2027.
      
     Pursuant to the provisions of the Ordinance that have come into operation, the Secretary for Development has published the plan (numbered NM/001) concerning the area of the Northern Metropolis delineated for the Ordinance in the following website (www.nm.gov.hk/en/about-nm/nmdevelopmentordinance). A copy has also been made available in the office of the Land Registry for inspection by the public free of charge during opening hours (see www.landreg.gov.hk/en/services/services_d.htm for details).

item.title: Welcome remarks by SDEV at luncheon session of 2nd International Infrastructure and Projects Leaders Summit (English only)
item.description:
​Following are the welcome remarks by the Secretary for Development, Ms Bernadette Linn, at the luncheon session of the 2nd International Infrastructure and Projects Leaders Summit today (November 20):
     
Distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, 

Welcome

     I am delighted to extend a warm welcome to all of you joining us today for the 2nd International Infrastructure and Projects Leaders Summit (IIPLS). This summit also serves as the opening of the inaugural InfraEX Week 2026. I would like to express my sincere gratitude to all our speakers in the morning session and our government representatives for your insightful sharing, which perfectly fits into the theme of the summit "Envisioning a Sustainable Future: From Insights to Impacts".

Outcome of 1st IIPLS and opportunities of 2nd IIPLS
     
     Two years ago, we successfully hosted the inaugural summit. The inaugural event laid a solid foundation for broader and deeper international collaboration and strategic partnerships.

     I am happy to give you an update of what we have achieved over the past two years since the first summit. Hong Kong has risen to the second place globally in overall competitiveness and we have secured the fourth place in the aspect of "Basic Infrastructure" in the latest IMD World Competitiveness Yearbook. In addition, Hong Kong's position in an international construction cost ranking is continuously improving from the third place globally in 2020 to the ninth place in 2024 and further down to the 16th place this year. To avoid any misunderstanding, for this cost ranking index, having a lower rank is an improvement, and we have significantly improved. Through comprehensive strategies, we expect to achieve an overall reduction of over 10 per cent in our public works construction costs annually, amounting to $12-15 billion in the coming few years.

     This year's summit once again brings together distinguished experts, senior government officials, and industry leaders from around the world to Hong Kong, the international infrastructure centre. While you are joining the summit, we do not want to lose any opportunities, so we are also joining hands with the University of Hong Kong and the Construction Industry Council to enable better synergy for open dialogue and close collaboration.

National 15th Five-Year Plan and Hong Kong's First Five-Year Plan
     
     This year marks the opening year of the National 15th Five-Year Plan and Hong Kong's First Five-Year Plan. As we proactively integrate into and serve overall national development under "one country, two systems", we remain committed to fulfilling our role as a "super-connector" and "super value-adder". Specifically, we strive to facilitate the internationalisation of national standards and showcase our nation's innovation and technology to the world. In doing so, we are driving the systematic transformation and upgrading of the construction industry toward advanced, intelligent, and high-quality development. 

Expediting Northern Metropolis development
     
     At the heart of our local development strategy is the Northern Metropolis, which is a new impetus for Hong Kong in developing new quality productive forces. Adopting a planning-oriented and infrastructure-led approach, we are committed to producing about 900 hectares of spade-ready sites in the coming five years. And in the coming five years, we are also committed to delivering over 70 000 residential units, and providing one million square metres of new economic floor space. This mega development in the Northern Metropolis serves as a vital strategic vehicle for housing, innovation and technology, and industry integration.

AI, advanced technology and standards
     
     To deliver these projects efficiently and in a sustainable manner, we are actively transforming our practices across the board. Beyond streamlining the approval processes, we are harnessing artificial intelligence and driving the widespread adoption of advanced construction materials and technologies. We now have what we call the Building Technology Research Institute, a setup wholly owned by the Government, yet outside the government bureaucracy. This institute will help us translate R&D outcomes into practical industry applications, advance standards, and conduct accreditation, certification, and testing. The new institute strongly complements our Construction Industry Council, a statutory body comprising stakeholders in the sector to promote good practices and advanced skills, basically striving for continuous improvement. Through these breakthroughs, our engineering pioneers are redefining productivity, safety, and environmental stewardship across the industry.
     
Future-ready workforce
     
     Technology and physical infrastructure alone are not enough. Building a sustainable tomorrow requires a talented, adaptable, and professional community. It is the people that matter. Cultivating a future-ready workforce which is equipped with digital literacy, engineering excellence, and cross-sector expertise remains central to our efforts in capacity-building.

     In this regard, leveraging Hong Kong's strength as a world city, the Centre of Excellence for Major Project Leaders under the Development Bureau has become a Belt and Road Capacity Building Platform and will further connect to the world. This Centre of Excellence will establish international branding, and share knowledge for shared prosperity with Belt and Road countries and beyond. We will continuously strengthen the role of the Centre in the coming years, with the vision of upgrading the Centre and reshaping it into a "Centre of Excellence for International Infrastructure Governance and Major Project Leaders".
     
Closing
     
     As we conclude our morning session today, we look forward to four dedicated plenary sessions in the afternoon that will delve deeper into different topics. Without further ado, I hope that you will enjoy the rest of the lunch, and fill up your stomachs for a thriving afternoon session.

     I wish you all an enriching and fruitful time at the summit and during the InfraEX Week. Thank you.

item.title: Welcome remarks by SJ at 16th Business of IP Asia Forum Concurrent Breakout Session (English only) (with photo)
item.description:
Following are the welcome remarks by the Secretary for Justice, Mr Paul Lam, SC, at the 16th Business of IP Asia Forum Concurrent Breakout Session "Turning Creativity into Economic Value: Clearing Legal Roadblocks in IP Commercialization" today (November 20):

Distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen,

     A very good afternoon. A warm welcome to the 2026 Business of IP (BIP) Asia Forum. I am delighted to open this thematic breakout session co-organised by the Department of Justice and the Hong Kong Trade Development Council.

     To set the stage, we must first look at the broader vision guiding our development. The National 15th Five-Year Plan prioritises accelerating innovation, strengthening intellectual property (IP) protection and utilisation, and supporting Hong Kong in deepening its status as an international legal and dispute resolution services centre, as well as a regional IP trading centre. Echoing this national strategy, the Chief Executive's 2026 Policy Address highlights the Government's all-front commitment to developing Hong Kong as a premier regional IP trading hub. Today's session timely explores how innovators and enterprises could capitalise on these macro policy objectives via IP commercialisation.  

The engine: IP commercialisation in action

     To see this vision in action, let's start from home - our local cultural and creative industries. As a cultural melting pot of East and West, Hong Kong has been accelerating the commercial development of these sectors through cross-sectoral and cross-genre collaborations of local IPs, enabling innovators and enterprises to confidently capitalise on our macro policy objectives.

     For instance, movie IPs are deployed to promote tourism. Building on the resounding success of a Hong Kong movie, "Twilight of the Warriors: Walled In", 《九龍城寨之圍城》, the Hong Kong Tourism Board collaborated with the movie producer to launch an exhibition titled "Live out the Cinematic Charm of Hong Kong" in the name of that movie, where merchandise vendors offered classic dishes, nostalgic toys and movie merchandise on-site. This demonstrates how cultural buzz can be converted into tangible economic value.

     Another example is the Hong Kong Palace Museum's recently concluded special exhibition, "Ancient Egypt Unveiled: Treasures from Egyptian Museums", which attracted over 670 000 visitors. The Museum launched around 170 original merchandise items inspired by ancient Egyptian civilisation, such as the black cat plush and blind box. These products have generated more than $33 million in revenue for the Museum. The Museum's original IP, Pharaoh Cat, became a sold-out hit. You may recall having seen this cat at MTR stations and on KMB buses.

     To further lower the costs of IP transactions and facilitate IP trading, the Government introduced the Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Tax Deductions for Intellectual Property Expenditure) Bill 2026 into the Legislative Council last month. This Bill would implement tax-deduction arrangements for capital expenditure incurred by enterprises for purchasing eligible IP rights, or for the licence to use eligible IP rights. By reducing the tax associated with IP acquisition, we aim to encourage more enterprises to actively invest in IP development and commercialisation, thereby injecting stronger momentum into Hong Kong's development as a premier regional IP trading hub.

The shield: a robust IP protection regime

     We must recognise that the fruits of IP can truly flourish only when backed by solid legal safeguards. Safeguarding IP rights acts as a vital shield for innovation; it is the cornerstone for fostering technological development and allowing creators to safely monetise their work.

     Hong Kong possesses a robust legislative framework protecting all forms of IP, including patents, trademarks, registered designs and copyright. As a World Trade Organization (WTO) member, our IP protection regime fully aligns with the international standards set forth in the WTO Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of IP Rights.    

     Guided by the strategic blueprints I mentioned earlier, we will advance the extension of suitable international IP treaties to Hong Kong in an orderly manner. Currently, we are proactively forging ahead with the preparatory work for implementing the Protocol Relating to the Madrid Agreement Concerning the International Registration of Marks in Hong Kong.  

     To ensure that the local registered designs regime follows the mainstream international practices and meets future local industrial development needs, particularly those driven by the new industrialisation and growth of the digital economy, we are proactively planning to update the relevant regime. The Government is formulating a code of practice addressing copyright issues and the application of legal principles relating to the development of generative artificial intelligence technology, serving as a vital reference for the industry.

The safety net: excellence in dispute resolution

     As global innovation rapidly develops and IP commercialisation expands across borders, commercial disputes inevitably arise. Hong Kong is well-positioned to provide pre-eminent IP dispute resolution services. Both our IP protection regime and dispute resolution services are well recognised and widely acclaimed by the international community.  

     According to the World Competitiveness Yearbook 2026, Hong Kong ranks seventh globally in IP rights. Building on this, and with the Central People's Government's support, Hong Kong signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) in September 2025 regarding co-operation on the WIPO Lex-Judgments database. Under the MOU, Hong Kong contributes leading IP judgments from the Judiciary to the database, facilitating the international IP community's access to such judgments, while showcasing the quality of Hong Kong's IP-related jurisprudence. By enhancing the global transparency of our IP legal regime, we instill greater confidence to international businesses and IP rights holders to invest, innovate and commercialise their assets in Hong Kong.

     Of equal significance is the pioneering Arrangement on Reciprocal Recognition and Enforcement of Judgments in Civil and Commercial Matters by the Courts of the Mainland and of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, which has been given effect by our local legislation. Hong Kong judgments on IP disputes are now generally recognised and enforceable in the Chinese Mainland. This marks an unprecedented breakthrough as it goes beyond the conventional international norms in the Hague Convention (Hague Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Judgments in Civil or Commercial Matters) which explicitly excludes IP matters.

     Moving onto arbitration, our arbitration regime and services are also globally recognised by the international legal community. According to the 2025 Queen Mary University of London International Arbitration Survey, Hong Kong ranks as the second most preferred seat for arbitration globally and the most preferred seat in the Asia-Pacific region.

     Our Arbitration Ordinance (Cap. 609) was amended in 2017 to expressly provide that disputes over IP rights, whether arising within or outside Hong Kong, are arbitrable, and that enforcing an arbitral award is not contrary to public policy solely because it involves an IP dispute. This enhancement gives Hong Kong a competitive edge over other jurisdictions in the region.  

     To maintain our edge, the Government is resolutely pressing ahead with initiatives to strengthen Hong Kong's status as a leading international arbitral seat, including enhancing our arbitration legislative framework. To ensure that such a framework remains competitive and stays at the forefront of international development, the Working Group on Arbitration Law Reform was established in October last year to review and make recommendations on amendments to the Arbitration Ordinance. Drawing on its recommendations, we have put forward proposed amendments to the Arbitration Ordinance and launched a one-month stakeholder consultation, and target to complete the relevant legislative amendments within next year.

     Earlier today, you may have attended sessions at the BIP Asia Forum on diverse topics covering IP financing, valuation and management. I trust that our session today will complete the picture, with our panel speakers discussing the benefits of resolving IP disputes through arbitration and sharing case studies. They will also discuss how IP commercialisation drives innovation and fuels the local cultural and creative industries in Hong Kong.

     Looking ahead, the Government will continue its multipronged strategy to support and strengthen the capability of different industries, including cultural and creative sectors, in utilising IP. Supported by our solid legal infrastructure, Hong Kong has every opportunity to cement its role as a leading international legal and dispute resolution services centre and a regional IP trading centre in the years ahead.

     On this note, I wish this Forum and today's session every success. Thank you very much.

item.title: Hong Kong Customs operation combats illegal importation of animals (with photos)
item.description:
Hong Kong Customs launched a special enforcement operation in November to combat illegal importation of animals and detected two suspected cases of illegally importing animals. Seven live cats and two live dogs were seized, with a total estimated market value of about $92,000. Seven people were arrested.

     Through cyber patrol and intelligence analysis, Hong Kong Customs discovered social media accounts promoting cross-boundary animal transport services. Suspecting that individuals were using illicit channels to import animals, Hong Kong Customs launched a special enforcement operation this month and stepped up inspections of high-risk passengers and cargo at various boundary control points. 

     During the operation, seven local residents were arrested, comprising three males and four females, aged between 33 and 56. Among them, two were suspected of illegally importing the animals, two were responsible for local delivery, while the remaining three were recipients. The arrestees have been released on bail pending further investigation.

     Investigations of the above-mentioned cases are ongoing and the likelihood of further arrests is not ruled out. All the seized animals have been handed over to the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department for follow-up action.

     Being a government department specifically responsible for tackling smuggling, Customs will continue to enhance co-operation and intelligence exchanges with other law enforcement agencies, and carry out targeted anti-smuggling operations at suitable times to disrupt relevant crimes.

     Customs reminds the public that importing animals into Hong Kong without a valid permit is an offence.

     Under the Rabies Regulation (Cap. 421A), any person found guilty of illegally importing animals, carcasses or animal products is liable to a maximum fine of $50,000 and imprisonment for one year upon conviction.

     Members of the public may report any suspected smuggling activities to Customs' 24-hour hotline 182 8080 or its dedicated crime-reporting email account (crimereport@customs.gov.hk) or online form (eform.cefs.gov.hk/form/ced002).

item.title: Inspection of aquatic products imported from Japan
item.description:
In response to the Japanese Government's plan to discharge nuclear-contaminated water at the Fukushima Nuclear Power Station, the Director of Food and Environmental Hygiene issued a Food Safety Order which prohibits all aquatic products, sea salt and seaweeds originating from the 10 metropolis/prefectures, namely Tokyo, Fukushima, Ibaraki, Miyagi, Chiba, Gunma, Tochigi, Niigata, Nagano and Saitama, from being imported into and supplied in Hong Kong.
 
     For other Japanese aquatic products, sea salt and seaweeds that are not prohibited from being imported into Hong Kong, the Centre for Food Safety (CFS) of the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department is conducting comprehensive radiological tests to verify that the radiation levels of these products do not exceed the guideline levels before they are allowed to be supplied in the market.
 
     From noon on November 19 to noon today (November 20), the CFS conducted tests on the radiological levels of 173 food samples imported from Japan, which were of the "aquatic and related products, seaweeds and sea salt" category. No sample was found to have exceeded the safety limit. Details can be found on the CFS's thematic website titled "Control Measures on Foods Imported from Japan" (www.cfs.gov.hk/english/programme/programme_rafs/programme_rafs_fc_01_30_Nuclear_Event_and_Food_Safety.html).
 
     In parallel, the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) has also tested 50 samples of local catch for radiological levels. All the samples passed the tests. Details can be found on the AFCD's website (www.afcd.gov.hk/english/fisheries/Radiological_testing/Radiological_Test.html).
 
     The Hong Kong Observatory (HKO) has also enhanced the environmental monitoring of the local waters. No anomaly has been detected so far. For details, please refer to the HKO's website (www.hko.gov.hk/en/radiation/monitoring/seawater.html).
 
     From August 24, 2023, to noon today, the CFS and the AFCD have conducted tests on the radiological levels of 276 812 samples of food imported from Japan (including 172 221 samples of aquatic and related products, seaweeds and sea salt) and 58 864 samples of local catch respectively. All the samples passed the tests.

item.title: Pre-hospital Stroke Diversion Scheme extended to all districts in Kowloon and Lantau
item.description:
The following is issued on behalf of the Hospital Authority:

     In line with the policy direction outlined in The Chief Executive's 2025 Policy Address, the Hospital Authority (HA) and the Fire Services Department (FSD) first implemented the Pre-hospital Stroke Diversion Scheme (Primary Diversion Scheme) in the New Territories East Cluster (NTEC) and the New Territories West Cluster (NTWC) late last year. Under the Primary Diversion Scheme, FSD ambulance personnel directly convey patients assessed as having suspected large vessel occlusion (LVO) stroke to designated HA hospitals within the respective service catchment areas for early treatment. The HA and the FSD announced today (November 20) that the Primary Diversion Scheme will be extended from the New Territories to all districts in Kowloon and Lantau Island starting from November 23 to benefit more acute stroke patients.
 
     Spokespersons for the HA and the FSD said that the Primary Diversion Scheme has yielded very satisfactory results since its launch nearly a year ago. By eliminating the time required for interhospital transfers, transportation and other procedures, the average time from ambulance departure to receiving treatment for each patient has been shortened by about 80 minutes, enabling patients to receive appropriate treatment sooner. After reviewing its effectiveness, the HA and the FSD will further expand the Primary Diversion Scheme in accordance with the policy direction outlined in The Chief Executive's 2026 Policy Address, so that more eligible acute stroke patients can be conveyed to designated hospitals for treatment as soon as possible.
 
     The FSD spokesperson said that the Primary Diversion Scheme will be officially extended to all districts in Kowloon and Lantau Island starting from 8.30am on November 23. Patients who meet the criteria under the pre-hospital stroke assessment will be conveyed directly by ambulance to Princess Margaret Hospital, Queen Elizabeth Hospital or Kwong Wah Hospital for treatment according to their service catchment areas. For instance, patients located in Lantau Island or Tsuen Wan will be conveyed directly to Princess Margaret Hospital; patients in Kwun Tong will be conveyed directly to Queen Elizabeth Hospital; and patients in Tseung Kwan O will be conveyed directly to Kwong Wah Hospital.
 
     In accordance with established guidelines, ambulance personnel perform a pre-hospital stroke assessment through standardised medical evaluations before conveying patients to hospitals. If a patient is suspected of suffering from LVO stroke, they will be conveyed directly to the designated HA hospital within the respective service catchment area for follow-up. This arrangement aims to ensure that critical stroke patients meeting specific criteria are promptly triaged to designated hospitals equipped with the corresponding treatment services, thereby saving time on interhospital transfers and duplicated assessments, and allowing patients to receive timely and appropriate treatment.
 
     The HA spokesperson stated that upon receiving notification from the FSD, the Accident and Emergency Departments (A&Es) of public hospitals will mobilise dedicated teams to arrange the necessary examinations and treatments for patients as quickly as possible. These include intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) or intra-arterial thrombectomy (IAT) when clinically suitable, with a view to restoring blood supply to the brain promptly, increasing the patients' chances of recovery, and reducing physical disabilities caused by stroke.
 
     The Primary Diversion Scheme was officially launched in the HA's NTEC and NTWC on December 15 last year. As at August 31 this year, a total of 145 patients with suspected LVO stroke were conveyed directly by ambulance to the two designated hospitals, namely Prince of Wales Hospital and Tuen Mun Hospital, for treatment. During the same period, another 556 suspected acute stroke patients in these two clusters were conveyed by ambulance to the A&Es of nearby public hospitals for treatment under the Pre-hospital Stroke Notification mechanism jointly operated by the HA and the FSD.
 
     Spokespersons for the HA and the FSD reminded the public that if individuals suspect themselves or someone nearby is suffering from a stroke, they should promptly attend the nearest A&E, where healthcare staff will immediately arrange for necessary assessments and examinations. When calling the FSD ambulance services, members of the public should co-operate with the professional assessments and decision of ambulance personnel, who will convey the patients to suitable hospitals for further examination and treatment.
 
     Currently, all public hospital A&Es can arrange appropriate treatment for stroke patients. Strokes can be generally classified into two types, namely hemorrhagic stroke and ischemic stroke, which require different treatment approaches. For ischemic stroke, all A&Es currently offer 24-hour IVT services. Meanwhile, Prince of Wales Hospital, Tuen Mun Hospital, Princess Margaret Hospital, Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Kwong Wah Hospital, Queen Mary Hospital and Pamela Youde Nethersole Eastern Hospital also provide 24-hour IAT services, supporting stroke patients across Hong Kong through a comprehensive service network.

item.title: Grading of beach water quality released
item.description:
The Environmental Protection Department (EPD) today (November 20) released the latest grading of water quality for 11 gazetted beaches that are open for swimming in November.
 
     Eight beaches were rated as Good (Grade 1) and three as Fair (Grade 2).
 
Grade 1 beaches are:          
Big Wave Bay Beach Middle Bay Beach
Clear Water Bay Second Beach Repulse Bay Beach
Deep Water Bay Beach Silver Mine Bay Beach
Golden Beach Stanley Main Beach
 
Grade 2 beaches are:
Casam Beach Silverstrand Beach
Lido Beach  
 
     Compared with the grading released last week, there was no change in the grading for these beaches.
 
     Under the present grading system, beaches are classified into four grades, namely Good (Grade 1), Fair (Grade 2), Poor (Grade 3) and Very Poor (Grade 4), according to the level of E. coli in the water. Grades are calculated on the basis of the geometric mean of the E. coli counts on the five most recent sampling occasions.
 
     While the ratings represent the general water quality at the beaches, an EPD spokesman reminded members of the public that water quality could be temporarily affected during and after periods of heavy rain. Bathers should avoid swimming at beaches for up to three days after a tropical cyclone or heavy rainfall.
 
     A summary of beach grades is published weekly before the weekend. The latest beach grades based on the most current data may be obtained from the EPD's website on Beach Water Quality (www.epd.gov.hk/epd/beach) or the beach hotline, 2511 6666.  Members of the public can also obtain the latest daily water quality forecast information for all beaches that are open for swimming through the EPD's dedicated webpage on the beach water quality forecast (www.epd.gov.hk/en/BWQForecast).

item.title: Judiciary commences mandatory use of iCMS for civil proceedings in High Court and District Court
item.description:
The following is issued on behalf of the Judiciary:
 
     The Judiciary announced today (November 20) the commencement of the mandatory use of the integrated Court Case Management System (iCMS) for civil proceedings in the High Court and the District Court following the promulgation of e-Practice Direction 5. The mandatory requirement will apply to the High Court from November 27, 2026, and the District Court from December 21, 2026.
 
     The iCMS is an integral part of the Judiciary's Information Technology Strategy Plan. It aims to facilitate the electronic handling of court-related documents and payments across the various levels of court.
 
     As set out in the new e-Practice Direction 5, the mandatory use of the iCMS applies to all legally represented parties and institutional parties (including mainly government bureaux and departments, law enforcement agencies and statutory bodies) involved in e-proceedings in respect of all the iCMS-enabled case types (Note 1).  
 
     Starting from the respective commencement dates, applicable users must use the e-system to commence a proceeding or file a document for the iCMS-enabled case types. Originating documents or other filings submitted in conventional (paper) mode and payments in such cases will no longer be accepted by the High Court and the District Court.
 
     The mandatory use of the iCMS does not apply where the documents are exempted from the requirement, where permission has been given by the Court for using the conventional mode, and where a notice has been issued by the Judiciary for an unscheduled system outage or a technical problem which is not expected to be resolved within a reasonably short period ("Outage Notice") (Note 2). Furthermore, the mandatory requirement does not apply to proceedings or applications that are confidential in nature, including those relating to the Hong Kong National Security Law and the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance.
 
     In exceptional cases, an applicable user may apply to a Practice Master of the High Court or District Court for permission to commence a proceeding or file a document in the conventional mode, explaining the details of the technical problems, special circumstances, or urgency involved. The Practice Master may grant permission only if good cause is shown and doing so is in the interest of justice.
 
     Applicable users are reminded to ensure that e-filings are received by the Court within applicable time limits, taking into account factors such as system outage and other technical problems. 
 
     The e-Practice Direction 5, setting out its scope of application, exceptions and exemptions from mandated e-filing, and the procedures for consequential filing in the conventional mode, is accessible on the dedicated e-Courts webpage on the Judiciary website at www.judiciary.hk/en/e_courts/ref_practice.html.
 
     For enquiries, please email enquiry@judiciary.hk, call the technical helpline at 2886 6474, or contact the respective court registry for enquiries on the progress of e-filing:
 
  •           High Court Registry at 2825 0401
  •           Clerk of Court's Office (Civil and Criminal Registry) at 2825 4672
  •           Clerk of Court's Office (Appeals Registry) at 2825 4338
  •           District Court Registry at 2582 4274

Note 1: The iCMS currently covers selected case types of civil proceedings of the High Court, including civil appeal cases in the Court of Appeal, and commercial, construction and arbitration, intellectual property, personal injuries and civil action cases in the Court of First Instance; personal injuries action, tax claim, civil action and employees' compensation cases in the District Court.  
 
Note 2: Upon the issuance of an Outage Notice on the Judiciary's website, the mandatory e-filing requirement will be temporarily suspended. Users may then file documents in the conventional mode, accompanied by a valid Certificate of Outage downloaded from the website.

item.title: Hong Kong, China as regulatory member of International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use marks key step towards developing into international health and medical innovation hub
item.description:
The Health Bureau announced today (November 20) that Hong Kong, China has formally joined the International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) as a regulatory member. The ICH is a key international platform for the harmonisation of technical standards for drug regulation. Hong Kong's formal accession to ICH membership signifies international recognition of its drug research and development (R&D) as well as regulatory standards. It will help further promote the development of the capabilities and mechanisms for the "primary evaluation" of innovative drugs, enable Hong Kong to participate deeply in the formulation of international rules on drug R&D and registration, and accelerate the development of Hong Kong into an international health and medical innovation hub.

     At its assembly meeting held in Czech Republic on November 17, 2026, the ICH approved the admission of Hong Kong, China (represented by the Pharmacy and Poisons Board of Hong Kong) as its 20th regulatory member. Other ICH regulatory members include the National Medical Products Administration of China and the regulatory authorities of Europe, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and the United States.

     The Secretary for Health, Professor Lo Chung-mau, said, "The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) Government expresses its sincere gratitude to the country for its continued full support for Hong Kong's development into an international health and medical innovation hub. Hong Kong, China becoming an ICH regulatory member fully demonstrates the unique advantages of the 'one country, two systems' principle. Since becoming an ICH observer on October 31, 2023, Hong Kong has, with the country's strong support, devoted its full efforts to fulfilling all the requirements of the ICH, and was able to formally become an ICH regulatory member in just three years, significantly accelerating the process compared with the eight to 10 years estimated by the Government earlier with reference to international experience."

     Professor Lo added, "Looking ahead, the HKSAR Government will, in accordance with the First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (2026-2030), actively dovetail with the National 15th Five-Year Plan to support clinical R&D in biomedicine and optimise the evaluation and approval mechanism for innovative drugs, and drugs with urgent clinical use. The HKSAR Government will establish the Centre for Medical Products Regulation (CMPR) next month to build up capacity for independent drug evaluation and approval, and actively participate in international co-operation, with a view to developing Hong Kong into an international health and medical innovation hub and better integrating into and serving the overall national development."

     The Director of Health, Dr Ronald Lam, said, "Joining the ICH marks an important milestone in Hong Kong's drug evaluation, approval and regulatory reform, and is particularly significant to the CMPR to be established soon. The CMPR will, in accordance with the technical requirements of the ICH, build up a professional team for independent evaluation and approval, enhance the efficiency of evaluating innovative drugs, and deploy experts to participate in the formulation and revision of ICH guidelines, contributing to the scientific advancement of drug regulation worldwide. Hong Kong is now both an ICH regulatory member and a member of the Pharmaceutical Inspection Co-operation Scheme (PIC/S). The CMPR will adopt a science-based approach and strive to become an internationally renowned regulatory authority."

     The ICH is an authoritative international body for pharmaceutical harmonisation. The mission of the ICH is to harmonise global technical requirements for drug registration and to promulgate various guidelines on safety, efficacy and quality that are recognised as the highest international standards for the protection of public health. The PIC/S is a renowned international organisation comprising pharmaceutical regulatory authorities from multiple countries and regions. Its mission is to lead the international development, formulate standards for implementation, and adherence to harmonised Good Manufacturing Practice standards and quality systems among pharmaceutical regulatory authorities. Having passed the relevant assessment in 2015, Hong Kong, China formally became a PIC/S member with effect from January 1, 2016.

item.title: Latest Composite Waiting Time for Subsidised Rental Housing stands at 4.4 years, hitting 10-year low
item.description:
The Housing Bureau (HB) released today (November 20) that the latest Composite Waiting Time for Subsidised Rental Housing (CWT) is 4.4 years, a significant decrease of 0.4 years compared with 4.8 years as at end-June this year. Compared with the highest level of 6.1 years before the current-term Government took office, this marks a reduction of 1.7 years, falling below 4.5 years for the first time and hitting a new low in the past decade.
                     
     The latest CWT is calculated based on the average waiting time of general applicants (i.e. family and elderly one-person applicants) who were housed to public rental housing (PRH) or Light Public Housing (LPH) in the past 12 months as at end-September 2026.
      
     "With the continuous increase in overall public housing production and the progressive completion of various PRH and LPH projects, the long-standing backlogged applications have been gradually cleared, resulting in a downward trend in the CWT. We are confident that we can achieve the target of reducing the CWT to 4.5 years in 2026-27 as announced by the Chief Executive in the 2022 Policy Address," said a spokesman for the HB.
 
Overall public housing production entering harvesting phase
 
     Through the current-term Government's unremitting efforts for over four years to "enhance quantity, speed, efficiency and quality", a solid foundation for public housing production has been laid, which is now entering the harvesting phase. Looking ahead to the next five years (i.e. from 2027-28 to 2031-32), public housing, including PRH and subsidised sale flats, of more than 35 000 units per year on average will be provided, representing an increase of about 73 per cent compared with the five-year production since the current-term Government took office, the highest in the past 25 years. In respect of LPH, as of mid-November 2026, about 29 800 units have been completed. The remaining two new projects converted from school premises at Shun Lee Tsuen Road in Kwun Tong and Chuk Yuen Road in Wong Tai Sin (providing a total of about 210 units) are set to be completed in the first quarter of next year. All 13 projects providing about 30 000 LPH units will be completed in slightly over four years, ahead of the five-year target set out in the 2022 Policy Address. The huge housing supply has effectively shortened the PRH waiting time.
 
As many as 11 200 general applicants housed
 
     In the third quarter of 2026, a total of about 11 200 general applicants were housed to PRH or LPH, including about 3 100 newly completed PRH flats, about 2 700 recovered PRH flats, and about 5 450 LPH units. Of these, the number of applicants housed to LPH was more than four times that of the last quarter (about 1 300 units).
      
     "Over the past 12 months, the supply of PRH and LPH has significantly increased to an average quarterly supply of about 8 200 units, which is double the average quarterly supply of about 4 100 units during the four years before the current-term Government took office (i.e. from the third quarter of 2018 to the second quarter of 2022). The LPH has also reached the peak intake from July to September this year. In fact, the waiting time for general applicants who were housed to PRH in the last 12 months was 5.3 years, whereas the waiting time for general applicants who were housed to LPH during the same period was only 2.8 years on average, which fully highlights that the LPH policy has played a key role in enabling faster fulfilment of the grassroots citizens' housing needs, thereby effectively shortening the overall CWT," said the spokesman.
 
PRH waiting queue hits 15-year low
 
      "We are also making concerted efforts to adopt a multipronged approach to expedite the turnover of PRH flats. The number of PRH general applicants is on a downward trend, recording a further decrease of about 4 400 cases this time. We have also observed that many general applicants for the Urban district and Extended Urban district with a waiting time of six years or above were gradually housed to PRH, which tangibly reflects that our efforts over the past four-plus years are taking effect progressively," said the spokesman.
      
     As at end-September 2026, there were about 96 100 general applications for PRH, representing a significant decrease of nearly 40 per cent compared with the highest level of 156 400 cases as of September 2020, a new low over the past 15 years and also the first time the figure has fallen below 100 000 since 2012. Meanwhile, there were about 80 600 non-elderly one-person applications under the Quota and Points System, representing an even sharper decrease of over 40 per cent compared with the highest level of 143 700 cases as of December 2015. Of these, the drop in non-elderly one-person applicants aged below 30 was even more pronounced, falling by about 60 per cent over the past decade from about 70 400 as at end-September 2016 to about 29 300 as at end-September 2026. These figures clearly demonstrate that the PRH waiting queue is being cleared.

item.title: Film Programmes Office to launch screening programme "Made in Italy - A World of Bittersweetness" (with photos)
item.description:
The Film Programmes Office of the Leisure and Cultural Services Department will present the programme "Made in Italy - A World of Bittersweetness". Sixteen Italian films depicting the flavours of life will be screened at the Hong Kong Film Archive (HKFA) and K11 Art House from December 13, 2026, to January 24, 2027.
 
     Three of the selected works are romantic films, including "La Dolce Vita" (1960) starring the "Latin Lover" Marcello Mastroianni; "Girl with a Suitcase" (1961) featuring the stunningly beautiful Claudia Cardinale; and "Il Bell' Antonio" (1960), in which the two co-star.
 
     Films exploring the relationship between class struggle and social development in their works are also selected, including Francesco Rosi's "Hands Over the City" (1963), Bernardo Bertolucci's "The Conformist" (1970), and Elio Petri's "Investigation of a Citizen Above Suspicion" (1970) telling the story of police investigating a murder committed by a colleague.
 
     Moreover, the programme also features four works centring on family relationships. "Bicycle Thieves" (1948) tells of an unemployed father taking desperate risks for his family. In "The Son's Room" (2001), a psychoanalyst blames himself as his wife and daughter sink deep into the grief of bereavement. A father in "Misunderstood" (1966) conceals from his youngest son the death of his mother, ultimately leading to a tragedy. "Everybody's Fine" (1990) tells of a father's journey visiting his grown children scattered across the country.
 
     Three of the selected works are stories of war, including "Rome, Open City" (1945) filmed on location during wartime, "The Four Days of Naples" (1962), which recounts the residents of Naples rising up in revolt, and "Life Is Beautiful" (1997), which tells of a Jewish father and son imprisoned in a concentration camp.
 
     There are two other works themed on the perils of the underworld, including "The Traitor" (2019) based on a prominent Italian Mafia family and "Property Is No Longer a Theft" (1973), which tells of a bank cashier stealing ill-gotten gains from a butcher.
 
     The programme also features "Ennio" (2021), a documentary introducing the creative career of film score maestro Ennio Morricone. His compositions are in numerous classic films including "Investigation of a Citizen Above Suspicion", "Property Is No Longer a Theft" and "Everybody's Fine".
 
     All films are with Chinese and English subtitles. "The Traitor" is rated Category III and restricted to viewers aged 18 or above.
 
     Tickets for screenings at the HKFA are priced at $75 and are now available at URBTIX (www.urbtix.hk). For telephone bookings, please call 3166 1288. For screenings at K11 Art House, tickets are priced at $110 and $150 and are now available at K11 Art House and the website of MCL Cinemas (www.mclcinema.com). For programme enquiries and concessionary schemes, please call 2734 2900 or visit www.lcsd.gov.hk/fp/en/listing.html?id=101.
 
     Some screenings will be accompanied by post-screening talks hosted by Thomas Shin, Pierre Lam, Dr Sonia Au and programme curator Freddie Wong. In addition, three post-screening seminars, titled "Remembering Mastroianni: The 30th Anniversary of His Passing Away", "A Tribute to Italian Screen Goddess: Claudia Cardinale" and "Introducing Ennio Morricone: Grand Master of Film Music", will be hosted by Law Kar, Horace Chan and Dr Angela Law respectively. The post-screening talks and seminars will be conducted in Cantonese. Ticket holders of respective screenings will be admitted with priority. Seats will be available on a first-come, first-served basis.

item.title: Speech by FS at Canadian Indo Pacific Business Summit (English only) (with photos)
item.description:
Following is the speech by the Financial Secretary, Mr Paul Chan, at the Canadian Indo Pacific Business Summit today (November 20):

Assistant Deputy Minister Epp (Assistant Deputy Minister for the Indo Pacific, Government of Canada, Mr Weldon Epp), Consul General Charles Reeve (Consul General of Canada to Hong Kong and Macao), Goldy (President and Chief Executive Officer of the Business Council of Canada, Mr Goldy Hyder), Brett (Executive Co-Convenor of the Canadian Chambers of the Indo Pacific, Mr Brett Stephenson), Adam (Executive Co-Convenor of the Canadian Chambers of the Indo Pacific, Dr Adam Janikowski), Rosemary (Chair of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, Ms Rosemary Goater), Chairs of the Canadian chambers of commerce across the region, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen,

     Good morning, and welcome to Hong Kong. It is a great pleasure to join you at the first Canadian Indo Pacific Business Summit. We are honoured that the 21 Canadian chambers across the region, with their partners in Canada, have chosen Hong Kong as their host. You have timed it well too, in the same week that APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) leaders met just across the boundary in Shenzhen.

A long partnership
 
     The ties between Canada and Hong Kong are long-standing and close. About 300 000 Canadians live here, one of the largest Canadian communities outside Canada. More than 200 000 people in Hong Kong are graduates of Canadian universities. Canadian companies have been in Hong Kong for well over a century, and two of them, Sun Life and Manulife, now account for nearly 40 per cent of the assets in our Mandatory Provident Fund system.

Canada looks to Asia

     These ties matter more now, because Canada is widening its trade and investment across Asia. It has set the goal of doubling its exports to markets beyond the United States within a decade. In January, China and Canada established a new strategic partnership, and Canada aims to increase its exports to the Chinese Mainland by 50 per cent by 2030. Last week, Canada announced that it had substantially concluded free trade negotiations with ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations).

     And in Shenzhen this week, on the sidelines of APEC, China and Canada agreed to expand mutual tariff relief and to extend their trade arrangement to the end of 2028. As Prime Minister Carney (Prime Minister of Canada, Mr Mark Carney) said the next day, the relationship is "growing on every front".

     I had the pleasure of meeting Prime Minister Carney in Davos earlier this year. There, he said that Canada has what the world wants: energy, resources, talent and capital. A fast-growing Asia needs all four. And Hong Kong, as a "super connector" and "super value-adder", is where Canadian supply and Asian demand can meet.

     So today, I would like to share with you where Hong Kong is heading, and where we can do more together.

Where Hong Kong is heading

     Our economy is growing strongly. It expanded by 5.1 per cent over the first nine months, the fastest pace for that period in five years. Exports are leading the way: goods exports rose by 30 per cent in the third quarter, lifted by strong global demand for AI-related electronics.

     Domestic demand remains solid, with private consumption up by 2.9 per cent and investment up by 7.5 per cent in the third quarter. We forecast growth of 4.8 per cent for the year as a whole.

     Underlying inflation is low, at 1.7 per cent in the first nine months, and unemployment has edged down to 3.8 per cent. Home prices have risen by around 7 per cent this year, and the office market is stabilising. Capital keeps flowing in: bank deposits grew by nearly 8 per cent in the first nine months, to HK$21 trillion. Earlier this month, when global financial leaders met in Hong Kong, all expressed optimism about our prospects, and a number of them told us they intend to increase their investment and headcount here.

     Business sentiment is positive, and we are cautiously optimistic about the outlook for 2027.

     Behind these numbers are our enduring institutional strengths under the "one country, two systems" framework: bilingual common law system, a freely convertible currency with no exchange control, a simple and low tax regime, and a free port. Last month, the Fraser Institute in Vancouver again rated Hong Kong the freest economy in the world.

     Our rule of law is recognised internationally. In the latest World Justice Project Rule of Law Index, Hong Kong ranks 24th among 143 jurisdictions, and in the global top 10 both for absence of corruption and for order and security.

     Our development direction for the coming five years is set out in Hong Kong's First Five-Year Plan, published in September. It aligns with the National 15th Five-Year Plan, which supports Hong Kong's development as "four centres and one hub": international centres for finance, shipping, trade, and innovation and technology, plus an international hub for top talent.

     In the interest of time, I would just highlight two major themes in the Plan: finance, and technology and innovation. 

     On finance, we are building a more complete range of funding options for businesses, from private equity, venture capital, patient capital to the equities market. In the first 10 months of this year, 121 companies listed on our stock exchange, raising over HK$400 billion. We are also going beyond equities into fixed income, gold and commodities, and will further strengthen our leading position in offshore Renminbi business. 

     On technology, AI is leading the way. It is not simply another sector; it is transforming existing industries.

     Hong Kong's edge also rests on our synergy with the Greater Bay Area (GBA), which is one of the most competitive global innovation and technology hubs, supported by advanced manufacturing and commercialisation capabilities. For a new technology, the GBA is a testing ground, a production base and a market of 88 million people. 

     Our main platform for this collaboration is the Northern Metropolis on the border with Shenzhen.  There, we are settling down the technology companies attracted to Hong Kong and building three university towns so that cutting-edge research, start-ups and industries can flourish side by side. A company can take an idea from the laboratory to the factory, and on to the market, without leaving the GBA.

     A hotspot of this collaboration is Hetao, where a science park in Hong Kong and its sister park in Shenzhen work together across the Shenzhen River. There, we are piloting special policies to ease the flow of people, materials, capital and data between the two parks.

     Consider biotechnology and medicine, where these flows matter most. A clinical trial depends on patients, samples and data. At Hetao, we have established a joint clinical trial platform with Shenzhen, so that biological samples and medical data from the Mainland can be used in the Hong Kong park. The aim is to shorten the time of research breakthrough to outcome commercialisation, and to allow a technology company based there to serve both the Mainland and international markets.

     So what more can Hong Kong and Canada do together? I see three areas: capital, resources and innovation.

Capital, in both directions

     The first is capital. Canadian investors have long used Hong Kong as their base for Asia. As opportunities in Mainland technology expand, Hong Kong will remain the channel of choice through which Canadian capital can take part in that growth.

     Capital can flow the other way as well. Canada aims to catalyse CDN$1 trillion of investment at home over the next five years, in fields such as energy, critical minerals and artificial intelligence.

     Hong Kong is a natural place to help realise that ambition. We are Asia's leading asset and wealth management centre, with about HK$42 trillion under management at the end of last year. We are also home to more than 3 300 wealthy family offices. I encourage Canadian project sponsors to come here and make their case.

     Our capital markets offer another solution. Several Canadian companies are already listed in Hong Kong, and the Toronto Stock Exchange is among the exchanges that we recognise for secondary listings.

     Hong Kong also brings companies and innovation to Canada. In September, under our GoGlobal Task Force (Task Force on Supporting Mainland Enterprises in Going Global), Invest Hong Kong took a delegation of Mainland green technology and life sciences companies to Vancouver, Calgary and Edmonton. We encourage Canadian companies to work with Mainland enterprises as they go global, and to use Hong Kong as the meeting place.

Resources, and the services they need

     The second area is resources. Canada is one of the world's major producers of energy and metals, and about 40 per cent of the world's public mining companies are listed on Canadian exchanges. More of what Canada produces is being sold in this region. Canada now ships about 1 million tonnes of liquefied natural gas to Asia every month.

     Trade on that scale needs financing, hedging and settlement, and Hong Kong is building the capacity to provide all of them. In fixed income and currencies, we are developing the whole chain, from issuance, trading, clearing and settlement to the derivatives used to manage interest rate and currency risk.

     We are doing the same in commodities, starting with gold. Canada was the world's fourth largest gold producer last year, and Hong Kong is developing an international gold trading market, with services that run from storage and clearing to financing and risk management.

     For other metals, we have more than 20 warehouses approved by the London Metal Exchange. A bill before the Legislative Council would halve the profits tax rate for qualified traders of physical commodities, from energy and metals to canola. I hope Canadian producers, traders and their bankers will use these services to reach their customers in Asia.

Innovation and talent

     The third area is innovation and talent.

     Canada is one of the birthplaces of modern AI, and much of the pioneering research was done in its universities. Hong Kong's strength is in turning that science into applications. We offer an international environment for testing and applying these technologies, and what succeeds here can go on to succeed elsewhere.

     We are keen to attract the best tech enterprises to Hong Kong. To this end, we have set up the Office for Attracting Strategic Enterprises, and are willing and ready to put together dedicated packages comprising land grant, financial support and tax concessions for the right enterprises.

     None of this is possible without talent, and our doors are wide open. Since the end of 2022, more than 320 000 people have arrived in Hong Kong through our talent schemes, and we would welcome many more from Canada.

Closing

     Ladies and gentlemen, a business that commits to a market for the long term needs to know that the policies and rules will hold.

     In a world of growing uncertainty, Hong Kong remains a place of predictability and consistency. It is also a city of abundant opportunity.

     In 2027, the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region turns 30, and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong turns 50. Canadian companies, schools and families have contributed a great deal to Hong Kong through those years. For that, we are truly grateful.

     As Brett described in his invitation to me on this conference: Hong Kong is a champion for Canadian business in the region. We will remain exactly that: always open, always welcoming, and always ready to work with you, here and across Asia.

     I wish you a most successful Summit. Thank you.

item.title: CS chairs first meeting of Working Group on Coordination of AI Risk Governance (with photos)
item.description:
The Chief Executive announced in the 2026 Policy Address that the Chief Secretary for Administration, Mr Chan Kwok-ki, will co-ordinate the work of various bureaux in taking forward the artificial intelligence (AI) risk governance strategy. Mr Chan convened the first meeting of the Working Group on Coordination of AI Risk Governance (Working Group) today (November 20) to comprehensively advance the co-ordination work of the AI risk governance strategy.

     Mr Chan said that whilst AI is developing rapidly, promoting industry upgrades and improving the convenience of daily life, its impact on various sectors of society and the importance of risk governance and application safety are equally crucial. The Working Group will steer and co-ordinate the efforts of bureaux and departments to examine issues relating to AI development risks, governance and safety; strengthen risk awareness; and examine corresponding management and regulatory frameworks. The aim is to ensure that, whilst accelerating the adoption of AI applications, the technology is used for good and remains safe and under control.

     At the meeting, the Working Group reviewed and co-ordinated the work plans and implementation proposals for the seven specific actions under the AI risk governance strategy, including (1) combating the use of AI in criminal activities; (2) enhancing the protection of users who are minors; (3) promoting market assessment of AI ethical risks; (4) promoting the safe and orderly application of AI across industries; (5) examining legal liability arising from accidents caused by AI products; (6) introducing guidelines on AI agent management; and (7) examining the impact of AI on employment. 

     The Working Group will convene meetings regularly in accordance with the progress of work to review and oversee the progress made by bureaux and departments in implementing the various measures, and to co-ordinate interdepartmental matters, thereby ensuring that Hong Kong's AI risk governance strategy is implemented comprehensively, soundly and in an orderly manner.

     Members of the Working Group are: 

Chief Secretary for Administration (Chairman)
Secretary for Justice
Secretary for Education
Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury
Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry
Secretary for Labour and Welfare
Secretary for Security
Head, Chief Executive's Policy Unit
Commissioner for Digital Policy

     Representatives of other relevant policy bureaux and departments will attend meetings as necessary.

item.title: Research Grants Council to present public lecture on "Exploring the Universe"
item.description:
The following is issued on behalf of the University Grants Committee:

     Pursuant to the Government's initiative to bolster STEAM (science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics) education at the primary and secondary school levels, as well as to step up efforts in identifying and nurturing local STEAM talent, the Research Grants Council (RGC) will organise a series of public lectures in November. Various topics including artificial intelligence and universe exploration will be covered. Admission is free on a first-come, first-served basis. All are welcome.

     The final lecture titled "Exploring the Universe" will be held on November 28 (Saturday). The lecture will be conducted in Cantonese. Details are as follows:

Time: 2.30pm to 4.30pm
Venue: Lecture Hall, 1/F, Hong Kong Science Museum
Live Broadcast:  Facebook page (www.facebook.com/hkscm) or YouTube channel (www.youtube.com/user/hksciencemuseum) of the Hong Kong Science Museum

Session 1: "Supernovae: Remarkable Cosmic Fireworks"
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     Supernovae are among the most spectacular explosions in the universe, marking the dramatic deaths of stars. These cosmic fireworks release enormous energy, briefly outshining entire galaxies and seeding the cosmos with heavy elements essential for planets and life. Long after the explosion fades, expanding supernova remnants sculpt the interstellar medium, accelerate cosmic rays, and trigger new generations of star formation. This talk, presented by Associate Professor in the Department of Physics at the University of Hong Kong Professor Stephen Ng, will introduce the physics behind stellar explosions and the stunning remnants they leave behind, uncovering why they are the most captivating frontiers in modern astrophysics, and highlight the recent results from supernova research.

Session 2: "A New Era of Space Exploration: Unlocking the Mysteries of the Universe"
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     With the rapid development of technology, humanity is in a golden age of space exploration. This talk, presented by Associate Professor in the Department of Science and Environmental Studies at the Education University of Hong Kong Dr Chan Man-ho, will introduce several current and upcoming space missions, including those initiated by the country. These missions aim to address some major enigmas about the universe, such as the mysteries of the solar system and the problems of dark matter, dark energy, and the standard cosmological model. The lecture will examine how space missions can help unlock these mysteries and reshape understanding of the universe.

     The RGC has been regularly organising public lectures since 2009, featuring various distinguished scholars as speakers. These lectures aim to promote research knowledge from Hong Kong's tertiary institutions and raise public awareness of the significance and value of local research work.

     For enquiries, please call 2524 3987 or visit the University Grants Committee webpage (www.ugc.edu.hk/eng/rgc/about/events/lectures/lectures.html). Additionally, members of the public can register for the RGC's email subscription service at www.ugc.edu.hk/eng/rgc/about/subscribe to receive regular updates.

item.title: CHP reminds public to take precautions against cold weather
item.description:
The Centre for Health Protection (CHP) of the Department of Health (DH) today (November 20) reminded the public, particularly the elderly, people with chronic illnesses, outdoor workers, pregnant women, infants and children, to adopt appropriate measures to protect their health in view of the cold weather.
     
Elderly and people with chronic illnesses
---------------------------------------------
     A spokesman for the CHP said that in general, elderly people have less insulating fat, and their body temperature control mechanisms would be weaker. Their body may not respond appropriately to the cold weather. In addition, some senior persons may have decreased mobility, which can impair their ability to generate and conserve body heat.

     Chronic illnesses, such as hypertension, diabetes or hypothyroidism, would lower their metabolic rate, subsequently causing their body to generate less heat. Besides, persons with chronic illnesses, such as chronic respiratory illnesses or cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, are vulnerable to disease aggravation due to cold weather.

     The spokesman reminded the public, in particular the elderly and persons with chronic illnesses, to adopt the following preventive measures:
 
  • Take note of the weather forecast. Wear warm clothing, including hats, scarves, gloves and socks, accordingly;
  • Consume sufficient food to ensure adequate calorie intake;
  • Perform regular exercise to facilitate blood circulation and heat production;
  • Stay in a warm environment. Avoid going out in the morning and at night when the temperature is lower, and avoid prolonged outdoor exposure;
  • Use heaters with care and maintain adequate indoor ventilation;
  • Avoid alcoholic beverages. Drinking alcohol cannot keep you warm. Alcohol accelerates the loss of body heat through dilated blood vessels, resulting in chilling instead; and
  • Seek medical advice if feeling unwell.

Infants, children and pregnant women
-------------------------------------------

     Infants and young children are more susceptible to heat loss during the cold weather. The spokesman reminded parents that they should ensure babies are sufficiently warm, but it is also important to keep babies relatively lightly clothed to avoid overheating them. When children engage in outdoor activities, their clothing should be adjusted accordingly, and changed quickly if soaked. Infants, young children and pregnant women should also try to avoid going out in the morning and at night when the temperature is lower.

     Parents should observe the following safety measures when putting their children to bed:
  • Keep the room well ventilated and at a comfortable temperature;
  • Always place babies on their backs to sleep. Leave their heads, faces and arms uncovered during sleep;
  • Babies do not need pillows. Place babies on a firm and well-fitted mattress to sleep. Avoid soft objects, pillows and loose bedding;
  • Let babies sleep in a cot placed near their parents' bed; and
  • Maintain a smoke-free environment.

Outdoor workers
-------------------

     Outdoor workers should take heed of the weather report and wear appropriate warm clothing for work. Clothing should be changed as soon as possible if soaked. When the Cold Weather Warning is in force, they should take appropriate precautions. They should take a break immediately and seek help and medical attention if feeling unwell.

General public
----------------

     In addition, many respiratory pathogens, including influenza and SARS-CoV-2, may have increasing activity and community transmission during winter. Seasonal influenza vaccination is recommended for all persons aged 6 months or above, except those with known contraindications. Persons at higher risk of getting influenza and its complications, including the elderly and children, should receive seasonal influenza vaccinations early. Please see details of the vaccination schemes on the CHP's website.

     A person who gets influenza and COVID-19 at the same time may become more seriously ill and would have a higher risk of death. It is important for elderly persons, especially those residing in residential care homes, to receive both a seasonal influenza vaccination and a COVID-19 vaccination. They should also receive an additional booster against COVID-19 according to recommendations as soon as possible. The public should also maintain good personal and environmental hygiene against respiratory illnesses and note the following:
 
  • Surgical masks can prevent transmission of respiratory viruses from ill persons. It is essential for persons who are symptomatic (even if having mild symptoms) to wear a surgical mask;
  • Wear a surgical mask when taking public transport or staying in crowded places. It is important to wear a mask properly, including performing hand hygiene before wearing and after removing a mask;
  • Avoid touching one's eyes, mouth and nose;
  • Wash hands with liquid soap and water properly whenever possibly contaminated;
  • When hands are not visibly soiled, clean them with 70 to 80 per cent alcohol-based handrub;
  • Cover the mouth and nose with tissue paper when sneezing or coughing. Dispose of soiled tissue paper properly into a lidded rubbish bin and wash hands thoroughly afterwards;
  • Maintain good indoor ventilation;
  • When having respiratory symptoms, wear a surgical mask, refrain from work or attending classes at school, avoid going to crowded places and seek medical advice promptly; and
  • Maintain a balanced diet, exercise regularly, take adequate rest, do not smoke and avoid overstress.
     
     ​Food-borne diseases, particularly those linked to hotpot cuisine, are also common in cold weather. The following preventive measures should be taken:
     
  • Wash hands before handling and consuming food;
  • Do not patronise unlicensed vendors or those with poor hygienic standards while selecting food;
  • Wash and cook all food thoroughly;
  • Vegetables should be washed thoroughly in clean running water before cooking and consumption. When appropriate, scrub vegetables with hard surfaces with a clean brush to remove dirt and substances, including pesticide residues and contaminants, from surfaces and crevices;
  • Shrimps should be fully cooked until the shells turn red and the flesh turns white and opaque;
  • For shellfish such as scallops and geoduck, scrub the shells thoroughly and remove internal organs;
  • Do not eat any undercooked freshwater aquatic products. To ensure that the food is thoroughly cooked, the centre of the food should reach a temperature of at least 75 degrees Celsius so as to destroy pathogens;
  • Most hotpot ingredients should be stored in a refrigerator at 4 degrees C or below, while frozen food should be stored in a freezer at -18 degrees C or below;
  • Never use raw eggs as a dipping sauce for hotpot; and
  • Use different sets of chopsticks to handle raw and cooked food to avoid cross-contamination.
     
     ​​In addition, when using fuel-burning appliances, especially in indoor areas, the public should ensure adequate ventilation to avoid harmful exposure to carbon monoxide (CO) and prevent CO poisoning.
     
     For more health information, the public may call the DH's Health Education Infoline (2833 0111) or visit the CHP's website and Facebook Fanpage as well as press releases of the Labour Department on precautions against cold weather for outdoor workers and their employers when the Cold Weather Warning is in force.

     The public may also call Dial-a-Weather (1878 200) or visit the website of the Hong Kong Observatory for the latest weather information and forecasts, or its page on Weather Information for Senior Citizens.
