item.title: DH urges public to adopt healthy lifestyle to prevent lung cancer in support of Lung Cancer Awareness Month
item.description:
The Centre for Health Protection (CHP) of the Department of Health (DH) today (November 18) called on the public to adopt a healthy lifestyle and take effective measures to prevent lung cancer, in support of Lung Cancer Awareness Month.
      
     "The Government attaches great importance to cancer prevention and control. It has long adopted a multipronged approach comprising prevention, surveillance and promotion of healthy lifestyles to achieve the goal of 'early prevention, early detection and early treatment'. The relevant cancer prevention and control efforts have yielded remarkable results. Over the past decade, the survival rate for lung cancer has improved markedly, with the five-year relative survival rate nearly doubled, rising from 16.4 per cent in 2010 to 2013 to 30.9 per cent in 2018 to 2022. Nevertheless, lung cancer remains the most common cancer and the leading cause of cancer deaths in Hong Kong," the Controller of the CHP, Dr Edwin Tsui, said.
      
Learn more about the most prevalent cancer in Hong Kong
------------------------------------------------------------------------
      
      Lung Cancer Awareness Month is designated in November every year to raise public awareness of lung cancer and promote the importance of prevention to alleviate the heavy health burden posed by lung cancer to the global population. In Hong Kong, lung cancer has long been the most common cancer and the leading cause of cancer deaths. In 2023, there were over 6 100 newly diagnosed lung cancer cases in Hong Kong, accounting for 16.1 per cent of all new cancer cases. Meanwhile, nearly 3 900 people died from lung cancer, with an average of more than 10 deaths per day. This accounts for over a quarter of all cancer deaths in Hong Kong.
      
     Early-stage lung cancer often has no obvious symptoms. Many patients do not seek medical attention until they experience severe discomfort, such as a persistent cough or coughing up blood, recurrent chest or lung infections, shortness of breath, chest pain, or hoarseness. By the time of diagnosis, the disease has often progressed to the intermediate or advanced stages. The five-year relative survival rate for Stage I lung cancer patients in Hong Kong is 72.4 per cent, while that for Stage IV patients is only 7.8 per cent, indicating that early detection is crucial for improving treatment outcomes. In addition to paying attention to changes in their physical condition, members of the public must prioritise disease prevention.
      
High-risk factors
---------------------
      
     Smoking is the leading risk factor for lung cancer, but it is also the most preventable. Compared to non-smokers, female smokers face approximately twice the risk of lung cancer, while male smokers face approximately four times the risk. Conventional cigarettes and other tobacco products release harmful substances and carcinogens. There is no safe level of smoking. The greater the cigarette consumption, the earlier the initiation and the longer the duration of smoking, the greater the risk of developing lung cancer.
      
     Furthermore, prolonged exposure to secondhand smoke (including at home, in the workplace and in public spaces) also significantly increases the risk of developing lung cancer. Other risk factors include advanced age, air pollution, occupational exposure to carcinogens (such as radon gas and asbestos), a history of lung diseases (such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) and a family history of lung cancer, especially if a first-degree relative has had the disease.
      
Evidence-based lung cancer screening study
-----------------------------------------------------
      
     The Cancer Expert Working Group on Cancer Prevention and Screening (CEWG) regularly reviews local and international scientific evidence to recommend evidence-based measures to the Government for cancer prevention and screening applicable to the local population. At present, the CEWG does not recommend routine lung cancer screening for asymptomatic individuals at average risk. The Chief Executive announced in the 2025 Policy Address the enhancement of cancer screening technologies through commissioning local universities to explore the use of AI-aided lung cancer screening. Currently, a three-year study was launched in January 2026 to explore the feasibility of using AI to assist lung cancer screening for high-risk individuals and offer local evidence for future lung cancer screening strategies in Hong Kong.
      
Lung cancer prevention
--------------------
      
     Stay away from tobacco and quitting smoking are the most effective ways to prevent lung cancer. The Government has been adopting a multipronged and progressive approach, including legislation, enforcement, taxation, publicity and education, and smoking cessation services, to promote tobacco control, with a view to lowering the smoking prevalence continuously, which not only helps lower the incidence of smoking-related diseases, but also saves thousands of lives each year and significantly alleviates the burden of cancer and chronic diseases. The DH urged smokers to take immediate action to quit smoking and stay away from all smoking products. Non-smokers should also never start smoking out of curiosity, social pressure or the misconception that alternative smoking products, such as e-cigarettes, are "safer".
      
     The DH operates an integrated Smoking Cessation Hotline (1833 183) to handle general enquiries about smoking cessation and provide professional counselling and referral services. Members of the public can visit the smoking cessation thematic website (www.livetobaccofree.hk) for more information on smoking cessation and related support tools and services. They can also download the "Quit Smoking App" to keep track of their quitting progress and obtain tips on fighting cravings to maintain a tobacco-free life.
